title: 07 — Fine-Tuning and LoRA
html:
07 — Fine-Tuning and LoRA

The one idea: fine-tuning changes a pre-trained model's weights with your own examples. LoRA does it by freezing the original weights and learning a small low-rank correction, so a few percent of the parameters do the work. Reach for it only after prompting and retrieval are exhausted, and judge it on a frozen evaluation set.

1. What it is

Approach Changes When
Prompting Nothing in the model. Only the instructions and examples First, always
Retrieval (RAG) Nothing in the model. Relevant text is added to the prompt The model lacks facts or documents
Full fine-tuning All weights Rarely: expensive, risks forgetting
LoRA Small low-rank matrices beside frozen weights Teach a format, style or narrow task (extraction schema, classification labels)
QLoRA LoRA on a base model quantised to 4 bits Same, on smaller GPUs
Distillation Train a small model to copy a large one Cheaper self-hosted inference

LoRA, mechanically: a weight matrix W (d × d) stays frozen. Training learns A (d × r) and B (r × d), with small rank r. The layer then uses W + (α/r)·A·B.

  • B starts at zero, so training starts exactly from the base model.
  • After training, the adapter can be merged into W or kept separate.

QLoRA adds three things: 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantisation of the frozen base, double quantisation (quantising the quantisation constants too), and paged optimisers. NVIDIA's documentation notes that QLoRA trains slower than LoRA in exchange for its memory savings.

2. Why it matters

  • Self-hosted small models (3 to 14 billion parameters) often need fine-tuning to match a larger model on one narrow task, such as extracting fund fields or classifying rationale sentences.
  • Human corrections from review queues become training data. A fine-tuned adapter is the "self-learning loop" made concrete.
  • Every fine-tuned version changes outputs, so it needs evaluation, approval and versioning like any release.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: decide whether to fine-tune

---
title: Prompt, retrieve, or fine-tune?
---
flowchart TD
    S["Task not good enough"] --> P{"Better prompt and<br/>few-shot examples fix it?"}
    P -- "yes" --> DONE["Stop: no training"]
    P -- "no" --> K{"Missing knowledge<br/>or documents?"}
    K -- "yes" --> RAG["Add retrieval (RAG)"]
    K -- "no" --> F{"Narrow, stable task with<br/>hundreds+ good examples?"}
    F -- "yes" --> LORA["LoRA / QLoRA fine-tune<br/>on a frozen eval set"]
    F -- "no" --> MORE["Collect labelled data first"]

3.2 Intermediate: the dataset is the model

  • Format: instruction and response pairs (or chat turns) in exactly the form used at inference.
  • Quality over quantity: hundreds to a few thousand clean, diverse, human-checked examples usually beat a large noisy set.
  • Splits: train, validation and a frozen golden test set never used in training.
  • Leakage: remove near-duplicates across splits.

3.3 Senior: settings, evaluation, infrastructure

Setting Typical starting point (practitioner guidance, not a rule)
Rank r 8 to 64. Higher fits more but costs more
lora_alpha Often 16 or 2 × r. The scale is α/r
Target modules Attention projections (q, k, v, o), sometimes the MLP layers too
Learning rate Around 1e-4 to 2e-4 for LoRA, with warm-up
Epochs 1 to 3. Watch validation loss for overfitting
  • Evaluate per field and per label on the golden set (precision, recall, wrong-but-confident rates), not only by loss.
  • Compare against the base model plus a better prompt. A fine-tune that doesn't beat that is waste.
  • On Databricks (checked 2026-10-26): the managed Foundation Model Fine-tuning product is deprecated, with removal on 14 August 2026. Databricks points to AI Runtime, a serverless GPU environment for training and fine-tuning, as the replacement. Track runs with MLflow, and register adapters or merged models in Unity Catalog.
# Not run: requires transformers, peft and a GPU. The model name is a placeholder for an open-weight model.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("<open-weight-model>")
config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"], task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
model = get_peft_model(base, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()   # typically well under 1% of the base model

4. Working code

The script freezes a 256 × 256 layer, defines a target change of rank 4, and trains LoRA adapters of rank 1, 4 and 16 by gradient descent on the adapter matrices only. numpy only.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
d_in, d_out = 256, 256
W = rng.normal(0, 0.05, (d_in, d_out))              # a frozen, "pre-trained" layer
true_delta = rng.normal(0, 0.05, (d_in, 4)) @ rng.normal(0, 0.05, (4, d_out))  # the task needs a low-rank change
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (2048, d_in))
Y = X @ (W + true_delta)                            # what the fine-tuned layer should output

def train_lora(r, steps=1500, lr=0.02, alpha=8):
    A = rng.normal(0, 0.01, (d_in, r))              # LoRA: delta W = (alpha / r) * A @ B
    B = np.zeros((r, d_out))                        # B starts at zero, so training starts from the base model
    scale = alpha / r
    for _ in range(steps):
        err = X @ (W + scale * A @ B) - Y           # W itself is never updated
        g = X.T @ err / len(X)                      # gradient w.r.t. the effective weight
        A, B = A - lr * scale * g @ B.T, B - lr * scale * A.T @ g
    return float(np.mean((X @ (W + scale * A @ B) - Y) ** 2)), A.size + B.size

base_loss = float(np.mean((X @ W - Y) ** 2))
print(f"frozen base layer: loss {base_loss:.5f}, full fine-tune would train {W.size:,} parameters")
for r in (1, 4, 16):
    loss, params = train_lora(r)
    print(f"LoRA rank {r:2d}: loss {loss:.5f}, trainable parameters {params:,} ({params / W.size:.1%} of full)")

Output:

frozen base layer: loss 0.00608, full fine-tune would train 65,536 parameters
LoRA rank  1: loss 0.00413, trainable parameters 512 (0.8% of full)
LoRA rank  4: loss 0.00000, trainable parameters 2,048 (3.1% of full)
LoRA rank 16: loss 0.00000, trainable parameters 8,192 (12.5% of full)

What to notice:

  • Rank 1 is too small for a rank-4 change, and the loss stays above zero. Rank 4 matches it exactly with 3.1% of the parameters. Rank 16 also fits, but trains four times more parameters for no gain.
  • W is never updated. Only A and B change, which is why adapters are small to store and swap.
  • B starts at zero, so step zero reproduces the base model exactly.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Fine-tuning to add facts. Use retrieval. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and format.
  2. No frozen evaluation set. You can't tell better from different.
  3. Training data in a different format from inference prompts.
  4. Sending sensitive documents to outside fine-tuning services. Keep training in your perimeter, and redact.
  5. Ignoring the deprecation of managed fine-tuning products. Check status before building on one.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

  1. Change the true update to rank 8, and find the smallest LoRA rank that fits it.
  2. Add noise to Y and watch whether higher ranks start fitting noise (compare against a held-out X).
  3. Write a one-page evaluation plan for fine-tuning a small model to extract five factsheet fields.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does LoRA train, and what does it freeze?
  2. Why initialise B to zero?
  3. What three techniques does QLoRA add?
  4. When is retrieval better than fine-tuning?
  5. What happened to Databricks Foundation Model Fine-tuning, and what replaces it?

Answers

  1. It trains the low-rank matrices A and B. The base weights W are frozen.
  2. So the adapter's contribution starts at zero, and training begins exactly from the base model.
  3. 4-bit NormalFloat quantisation, double quantisation, and paged optimisers.
  4. When the model lacks knowledge or documents, rather than a behaviour or format.
  5. It is deprecated, with removal on 14 August 2026. Databricks recommends AI Runtime (serverless GPU) instead.

8. Sources
